title: Reading the classics
hook: read the best books first, or you may not get to them (Walden 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, simplify: a life frittered away by detail, and room cleared for the essential. Your line was simplify.

A stack by the bed. A great book someone meant to finish, the bookmark stalled near the start. On top of it, the phone, which is easier to pick up. Thoreau lived in a one-room cabin with very little furniture, and yet the third chapter of Walden isn't about saws or beans. It's called Reading. And in his earlier river book, he left advice that sounds simple and stings a little: read the best books first, or you may never get to them at all.
screen: `THE STACK BY THE BED.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED READING.` → `THE BEST BOOKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the order of things. The best books first is a line about time. Life is short, and reading hours are few. Fill them with whatever's nearest, and the great things wait forever. It's yesterday's simplify, applied to a bookshelf. Second, how to read: "Books must be read as deliberately and reservedly as they were written." Slowly, with attention, one considered sentence at a time. He compares real reading to a kind of exercise, something that asks you to stand on tiptoe, not something to doze over. Third, the book on the table. Thoreau tells us he kept Homer's Iliad on his table through the summer at the pond, and looked at it only now and then, because there was a house to finish and beans to hoe. The great book sat there, and he didn't read it as much as he meant to. That honesty is part of the lesson. Even Thoreau had a stack. Fourth, what a book can do: "How many a man has dated a new era in his life from the reading of a book." A whole new era, starting from a page. Not every book does that, but you can't know which one will unless you open it. That's the reason for the best books first: not to be impressive, but so the book that might change your life gets its chance.

segments.voice: If a book you consider great is within reach, open it anywhere and read one page, slowly, as deliberately as it was written; if not, bring to mind a sentence from any book that once mattered to you. Let one line stay, and turn it over. Notice a single word in it you'd hurried past before; you're not studying, just keeping company with it.
Reading the classics. Thoreau's chapter in Walden on reading slowly and deliberately, and his advice to read the best books first, because a single book can begin a new era in a life. Today's word.
Your line: the best books first. Reading hours are few, and worth guarding. That's day one thousand two hundred twenty-seven.
